fetched_contents.text: Effectiveness of interventions on early neurodevelopment of preterm infants: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background As preterm infants’ neurodevelopment is shaped by NICU-related factors during their hospitalization, it is essential to evaluate which interventions are more beneficial for their neurodevelopment at this specific time. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions initiated during NICU hospitalization on preterm infants’ early neurodevelopment during their hospitalization and up to two weeks corrected age (CA). Methods This systematic review referred to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses [PRISMA] guidelines and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42017047072). We searched CINAHL, MEDLINE, PubMed, EMBASE (OVID), Cochrane Systematic Reviews, CENTRAL, and Web of Science from 2002 to February 2020 and included randomized controlled/clinical trials conducted with preterm infants born between 24 and 366/7 weeks of gestation. All types of interventions instigated during NICU hospitalization were included. Two independent reviewers performed the study selection, data extraction, assessment of risks of bias and quality of evidence. Results Findings of 12 studies involving 901 preterm infants were synthesized. We combined three studies in a meta-analysis showing that compared to standard care, the NIDCAP intervention is effective in improving preterm infants’ neurobehavioral and neurological development at two weeks CA. We also combined two other studies in a meta-analysis indicating that parental participation did not significantly improve preterm infants’ neurobehavioral development during NICU hospitalization. For all other interventions (i.e., developmental care, sensory stimulation, music and physical therapy), the synthesis of results shows that compared to standard care or other types of comparators, the effectiveness was either controversial or partially effective. Conclusions The overall quality of evidence was rated low to very low. Future studies are needed to identify interventions that are the most effective in promoting preterm infants’ early neurodevelopment during NICU hospitalization or close to term age. Interventions should be appropriately designed to allow comparison with previous studies and a combination of different instruments could provide a more global assessment of preterm infants’ neurodevelopment and thus allow for comparisons across studies. Trial registration Prospero CRD42017047072. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12887-021-02559-6. Keywords: Neurodevelopment, Preterm infants, Systematic review, Interventions, NICU, Meta-analysis Background Rationale Over the last decades, the increasing survival rates of preterm infants admitted in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit [NICU] have emphasized the importance of considering their neurodevelopmental outcomes [1]. Preterm infants are more likely to have significant short- and long-term neurodevelopmental impairments, since their brains go through a critical period of development and maturation between 24 and 40 weeks of gestation occurring mainly during their NICU hospitalization [2, 3]. Significant neurodevelopmental disabilities associated with neurosensory, motor, behavioral and cognitive outcomes may then arise shortly after preterm infants’ birth and last beyond school age and adolescence [4] given that neurocognitive impairments in infants born preterm are still reported in adulthood [5]. Many factors in the NICU environment may be congruent or incongruent with the preterm infants’ developing brain and consequently influence their neurodevelopmental outcomes. Environmental stimulation (i.e., light, noise) [2, 6–8], social interactions with parents [7, 9] and caregiving experience [2] are among influential environmental NICU factors. Interventions targeting these elements during NICU hospitalization should therefore foster preterm infants’ early neurodevelopment. Different interventions initiated during NICU hospitalization targeting some of these influential NICU factors with the objective of improving preterm infants’ neurodevelopment have been examined in previous systematic reviews. These interventions consist of developmental care a wide-ranging group of interventions to minimize preterm infants’ NICU environmental stress [10–12], including Neonatal Individualized Developmental Care Assessment Program [NIDCAP], which is an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities provided by professionals and infants’ family [13], noise reduction management, [14] in addition to interventions with parental involvement (i.e. NIDCAP, kangaroo care and developmental care) [15] and skin-to-skin contact [16]. The effectiveness of these interventions has been evaluated on the long-term neurodevelopment of preterm infants at 12 months or 24 months of age, providing important evidence. Yet, measuring the effects of interventions implemented during hospitalization only at one year of age and older raises concerns about confounding factors that may have occurred between NICU discharge and the timing of the assessments and that could have influenced the infants’ long-term neurodevelopment along with interventions. Neurodevelopmental assessments of preterm infants during NICU hospitalization are currently performed to predict long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes and plan early interventions [17–19]. A systematic review confirmed that neurobehavioral assessments of infants’ general movements (GMs) referring to the most common and complex spontaneous movements patterns [20] and infants’ posture and movements with the Test of Infant motor Performance (TIMP) [21] done before term corrected age [CA] are the most significant predictors of long-term neurodevelopment [18]. fetched_contents.text: Early interventions involving parents to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes of premature infants: a meta-analysis - Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE): Quality-assessed Reviews CRD summary This review found that different strategies promoting child development in pre-term infants showed an overall positive effect, lasting up to 36 months when there was parental involvement. Although the review was generally well conducted, the conclusions should be interpreted with some caution given the pooling of trials with variation in participants, interventions and outcome measures. Authors' objectives To ascertain whether early interventions teaching parenting skills, and/or involving parents in the hospital care of their pre-term baby, improve short-term and school-age neurodevelopmental outcomes. The review on which this report is based covered a range of other outcomes, but these were not the primary focus of the article and are not discussed in this abstract. Searching The following databases were searched: MEDLINE (1966 to June 2008), EMBASE (1980 to August 2006), CINAHL (1982 to July 2006), PsycINFO (1972 to June 2006) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (Cochrane Library, Issue 2, 2006). Search terms were reported. The search was not restricted by language. Reference lists of articles were also examined. Each article's key words were re-entered into a new search. An expert in neonatal follow-up reviewed the study for completeness. Study selection To be eligible, studies needed to be of preterm infants (less than 37 weeks gestational age or below 2500g weight at birth) and include an intervention involving parents to improve infant development. Eligible studies had to measure infant development by standardised scales; a list of eligible scales was provided. The onset of the intervention needed to be in the first 12 months of the infant's life. Eligible study designs were randomised or a quasi-randomised controlled trials, in which the intervention was compared with routine care or no intervention. The primary outcome was long-term neurodevelopment at 12, 24, 36 months and/or 5 years. Across the trials, infants ranged in prematurity, body weight and health status. Some trials had disease-specific inclusion criteria, whilst a small number were restricted according to parental demographics. Trials generally excluded infants with chromosomal abnormalities, congenital infections, major neurological problems, serious pathology, and history of maternal drug abuse. Interventions varied in their nature, period of application, intensity, setting and parental involvement. Trials took place in the neonatal intensive care unit, hospital setting and/or in the home. The full characteristics of the included trials were described in a separate online appendix (see URL for Additional Data, accessed March 2010). Articles were assessed for eligibility independently by two researchers. Assessment of study quality Methodological quality was assessed in terms of allocation concealment, blindness of intervention, completeness of follow-up and blinding of outcome assessment. Follow-up was categorised as either less than 85% or more than 85% of infants included in the last follow-up. Assessment of methodological quality was performed by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved by discussion with a third reviewer not participating in study assessment. Methods of synthesis Meta-analyses were performed, incorporating a random-effects model, for continuous data using the weighted mean difference (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity was assessed using the Χ2 and I2 statistics. Two subgroup analyses were pre-specified based on neonatal risk and type of intervention. Trials were grouped according to intervention type: Newborn Individualized Developmental Care and Assessment Program (NIDCAP), kangaroo care or any other developmental intervention. For neonatal risk, high-risk infants were defined as infants with brain structural abnormalities, special sensory abnormalities, specific motor abnormalities or chromosomal abnormalities; low risk was defined as infants with the absence of the preceding criteria. Publication bias was assessed using a funnel plot. Results of the review Twenty-five randomised controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the review investigating neurodevelopmental outcomes (n=3,509 children). Few trials described randomisation methods in detail, three reported clearly adequate allocation concealment; 21 of 25 blinded the outcome assessor. Four trials had 85% or more outcome data at the last follow-up point. At six months, scores on mental scales (six trials) and performance scales (four trials) were not significantly different between the treatment groups. At 12 months, scores on mental scales showed significant differences in favour of the intervention (WMD 5.57, 95% CI 2.29 to 8.86; 12 RCTs), as did scores on the performance scales (WMD 5.10, 95% CI 1.44 to 8.75; nine RCTs). At 24 months mental scales showed significant differences in favour of the intervention (WMD 7.59, 95% CI 3.51 to 11.67; seven RCTs), but the difference was not statistically significant for performance scales (four trials). At 36 months there was a statistically significant difference in favour of the intervention for mental scores (WMD 9.66, 95% CI 5.01 to 14.31; two RCTs) but performance scores were not evaluated. At five years (three trials) there was no statistical difference between treatment groups. Statistical heterogeneity was present at 12 and 24 months for mental scales, but not clearly present for other outcomes or time points. fetched_contents.text: Longitudinal Follow-Up of Children Born Preterm: Neurodevelopment From 2 to 10 Years of Age Abstract Objective: To investigate the rate and stability of impairments in children born preterm by assessing (1) early and school-age outcome in four developmental domains and (2) individual changes in outcome at both timepoints. Design: Prospective, longitudinal cohort study in children born in 2006–2007, <32 weeks' gestation. Follow-up at 2 and 10 years of age included standardized neurological, motor, cognitive and behavioral assessments. Children were categorized as having no, mild or moderate-severe impairment in these four domains. A composite impairment score was composed and the number of domains with impairments counted. For each child, individual outcomes at both timepoints were compared. Results: Follow-up at both time-points was available in 71/113(63%) children. At group level, there were no significant changes in the severity of impairments per domain. However, at individual level, there were less children with a mild abnormal composite score at 10 years of age (44 vs. 20%; p = 0.006), and more with a moderate-severe abnormal composite score (12 vs. 35%; p = 0.001). Especially children with normal/mild outcome at 2 years were likely to shift to other outcome categories over time. Conclusions: Children with early severe impairment are likely experiencing impairments later on, but early normal/mild abnormal outcomes should be interpreted with care, considering the large individual shifts over time. Long-term follow-up in all children born very preterm should therefore be continued to at least school-age. Keywords: preterm birth, long-term outcome, long term follow-up, longitudinal, premature birth, developmental domains Introduction Being born prematurely threatens a healthy development across the life course (1). With developmental challenges arising, or becoming more visible with increasing age and additional demands on the child's functioning, favorable outcomes at an early age do not necessarily reflect on a child's abilities later in life (2). In order to fully recognize the difficulties of children born preterm, it is important to follow them individually, through several developmental stages, and include a standardized assessment of multiple domains of functioning. While studies initially reported on major handicaps, including sensory deficits, cerebral palsy and cognitive delay, the focus has shifted over the past years to a broader range of milder impairments. Alongside, the assessment of impairment across multiple domains has received more attention and led to the understanding that children born preterm are prone to develop impairments in several domains of functioning at the same time (3). This combination of multiple (mild or severe) impairments in different domains might have a significant impact on functioning later on in life. Several follow-up studies have now reported on outcomes in longitudinal cohorts of children born preterm at two or more time-points, however the majority of them only reported outcomes at group level, discarding the possible existing variation at an individual level (2, 4–7). Studies that did report on individual developmental trajectories mainly focused on one specific outcome domain in cohorts of children born extremely preterm (<26 weeks gestation) and reported stable trajectories of unfavorable cognitive and behavioral outcomes, persisting into adulthood (8, 9). Prospective studies using standardized outcome assessments of individual trajectories over time in multiple developmental domains are limited. One study reported stable numbers of children with severe disabilities (cerebral palsy, moderate to severe impairment in neuromotor function, vision, hearing and/or cognition) between 6 and 11 years of age, with considerable variation in individual trajectories (10). Recently, a study by Taylor and colleagues (11) reported a weak relationship between neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 and 10years of age in a large cohort of infants born extremely preterm (<28 weeks gestation). In this study, a relatively high proportion of children had an improvement of their neurodevelopmental impairment classification between infancy and childhood. Combining knowledge on the outcomes at different time-points and the individual variation in multiple domains between 2 and 10 years of age is important, not only for children born extremely preterm, but also for those born very preterm (28–32 weeks gestation). On one hand, it will benefit the counseling of parents of children born premature by potentially identifying those at risk, and, on the other hand, it may support early intervention strategies to improve outcome. The aim of the current study was to investigate the rate and stability of impairment in a prospective cohort of children born preterm (<32 weeks' gestation) between May 2006 and November 2007, by standardized assessment of neurological, motor, cognitive, and behavioral outcomes at both 2 and 10 years of age. A second aim was to assess the composite impairment scores and to report on the co-occurrence of impairments by considering the number of affected domains for each child at both timepoints. The final aim was to assess the individual changes in outcome in the separate domains over time. This will give an insight in the rate and stability of impairments in preterm born children from toddler to school-age. Interventions tested and outcomes targeted

The evidence points to a broad family of parental stimulation interventions, with the most commonly named interventions in the search results being NIDCAP, kangaroo care, developmental care, sensory stimulation, music, and physical therapy [N1-F1]. One review also explicitly includes “early intervention programs designed to support parents in promoting the development of their preterm infant” and notes that interventions may vary in nature, period of application, intensity, setting, and parental involvement [N1-F2]. The same review further states that interventions in the NICU setting may include developmental care, NIDCAP, kangaroo care, and skin-to-skin contact, with NIDCAP described as an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities [N1-F1]. This suggests that many interventions are not merely generic stimulation programs, but are adapted or individualized for preterm infants through observational guidance and caregiving strategies [N1-F1].

Motor and neurodevelopmental outcomes measured

The search results show that motor and neurodevelopmental outcomes are measured using a variety of standardized tools. The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development are repeatedly referenced as key developmental assessment instruments, with the search results noting that the Bayley Scales are used for diagnosing developmental delays in early childhood and that they are used in follow-up studies [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5]. One search result specifically refers to the Bayley-4 as a standardized assessment tool [N2-R4], while another excerpt explicitly mentions the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, Screening Test-Gross Motor Subtest as a quick, inexpensive tool [N2-R5]. The broader intervention review also states that neurobehavioral assessments of infants’ general movements and Test of Infant Motor Performance (TIMP) are among the most significant predictors of long-term neurodevelopment, especially before term corrected age [N1-F1]. This indicates that motor outcomes are measured with both general motor assessments and more specific infant motor-performance tools, while neurodevelopmental outcomes are measured with standardized developmental scales [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].

Standardization versus adaptation

The evidence suggests that some interventions are standardized or at least guided by standardized protocols, while others are adapted for preterm infants. NIDCAP is described as an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities [N1-F1]. The same review also states that interventions may vary in intensity, setting, and parental involvement, and that the review pooled trials with variation in participants, interventions, and outcome measures [N1-F2]. This indicates that while some intervention models are structured and standardized, many are adapted to the specific needs of preterm infants and their families [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The motor-assessment evidence further shows that standardized assessment tools were used across trials, but the review itself notes that outcome measures differed across studies [N1-F2].

Overall, the interventions studied are mostly parent-involved or family-centered, often implemented in NICU or home settings, and they target a mix of motor and broader neurodevelopmental outcomes, with motor assessment relying on standardized tools such as the Bayley Scales and TIMP [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5].
node_outputs.N8:
Evidence base on intervention effects and consistency

Size and direction of observed motor benefits

The most direct evidence from the search results is mixed but generally suggestive of some benefit. One systematic review and meta-analysis found that NIDCAP was effective in improving preterm infants’ neurobehavioral and neurological development at two weeks corrected age, while parental participation did not significantly improve neurobehavioral development during NICU hospitalization [N1-F1]. For other interventions, the synthesis showed that effectiveness was either controversial or partially effective [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis of parent-involved interventions found that at 12 months, scores on mental and performance scales favored the intervention, and at 24 months, mental scales also favored the intervention, although performance scales were less consistent [N1-F2]. These results indicate a positive direction of effect, but not uniform across all outcomes or all intervention types [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Which study designs and populations showed stronger evidence

The strongest evidence appears to come from randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses, especially those using standardized assessment protocols. The NIDCAP meta-analysis and the broader parent-involved interventions meta-analysis both relied on randomized trials [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence is also stronger for infants with higher risk or for follow-up at 12 and 24 months, where differences were statistically significant [N1-F2]. The review further notes that high-risk infants showed a similar range of effects as low-risk infants, suggesting that the benefits may not be restricted to a narrow subgroup [N1-F2]. However, the evidence is weaker for later follow-up, with no statistical difference at five years in the meta-analysis [N1-F2]. This suggests that the most consistent effects are seen in short-term NICU and early postnatal follow-up, whereas longer-term evidence is less robust [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Limitations such as heterogeneity, sample size, or follow-up duration

The evidence base is limited by heterogeneity. The meta-analysis explicitly notes that the included trials varied in participants, interventions, and outcome measures, and that the review was conducted with pooled trials of varying design and outcome measures [N1-F2]. The same review also states that the overall quality of evidence was low to very low [N1-F1]. Sample sizes are uneven across studies: the NIDCAP meta-analysis combined three studies involving 901 preterm infants [N1-F1], whereas the parent-involved intervention meta-analysis included 25 randomized controlled trials with 3,509 children [N1-F2]. Despite this, the review still reports statistically significant effects at some time points, which suggests that the sample size is sufficient for some comparisons, but not necessarily for all subgroups or outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Follow-up duration is another important limitation. The review emphasizes that many interventions are evaluated at one year of age or older, raising concerns about confounding factors that may occur between NICU discharge and the timing of assessments [N1-F1]. The longitudinal follow-up paper likewise stresses that favorable outcomes at an early age do not necessarily reflect later abilities and that individual trajectories can shift over time [N5-F3]. This means that short-term gains may not reliably predict long-term outcomes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence base suggests some positive effects of early parental stimulation interventions on motor and neurodevelopment, but the direction and magnitude are heterogeneous, with stronger support for short-term randomized trials and less support for long-term follow-up [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Long-term developmental and neurodevelopmental follow-up

Whether motor benefits persist into later childhood

The evidence on long-term persistence is mixed. The longitudinal follow-up paper reports that children with early severe impairment are likely to experience impairments later on, but early normal or mild abnormal outcomes should be interpreted with caution because many children shift over time [N5-F3]. At the group level, there were no significant changes in the severity of impairments per domain between 2 and 10 years of age, but at the individual level, some children improved while others deteriorated [N5-F3]. The same paper also states that longitudinal follow-up should continue at least to school age, because early outcomes do not necessarily predict later abilities [N5-F3]. This suggests that motor benefits observed early may not persist uniformly into later childhood, and that some children may improve while others do not [N5-F3].

Which follow-up ages and assessment methods were used

Follow-up was conducted at 2 and 10 years of age, with standardized neurological, motor, cognitive, and behavioral assessments [N5-F3]. The review also notes that neurobehavioral assessments such as general movements and TIMP are used before term corrected age and are among the most significant predictors of long-term neurodevelopment [N1-F1]. The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Third Edition, are explicitly referenced as a tool used in follow-up studies of extremely preterm infants [N5-F4]. These assessments indicate that long-term follow-up uses both infant-specific motor-performance tools and standardized developmental scales, with follow-up ages extending into school-age [N1-F1][N2-R1][N5-F3].

Limitations for interpreting long-term outcomes

The main limitations are individual variability and the potential for confounding factors. The longitudinal study emphasizes that early normal or mild abnormal outcomes should be interpreted with care because many children shift over time [N5-F3]. It also notes that follow-up at one year of age and older raises concerns about confounding factors that may have occurred between NICU discharge and assessment [N1-F1]. The review further states that most follow-up studies report outcomes at group level rather than individual level, and that studies focusing on individual developmental trajectories are limited [N5-F3]. This means that long-term outcomes are difficult to interpret because they depend not only on intervention effects but also on changes in the child’s environment, health, and other developmental trajectories [N1-F1][N5-F3].

Overall, the follow-up evidence suggests that early motor gains may not persist in all children and that long-term outcomes should be viewed as highly variable, with standardized assessments used at 2 and 10 years of age, but with limitations from individual change and confounding factors [N1-F1][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
How intervention design features affect outcomes

Effects of timing, frequency, and dosage of stimulation

The evidence points to timing as an important design feature. The review notes that interventions initiated during NICU hospitalization were evaluated, and that effectiveness was measured during hospitalization and up to two weeks corrected age [N1-F1]. This suggests that interventions delivered early during NICU stay are the primary focus of the evidence base. The same review also emphasizes that many interventions are assessed only at one year of age or older, raising concerns about confounding factors occurring after discharge [N1-F1]. This implies that timing matters because early intervention may have different effects than later intervention. However, the evidence provided does not explicitly quantify frequency or dosage, so the timing effect is inferred rather than directly measured [N1-F1].

Effects of caregiver training and fidelity

Caregiver training and fidelity appear important, but the evidence is indirect. The review states that interventions may vary in intensity, setting, and parental involvement, and that the review pooled trials with variation in participants, interventions, and outcome measures [N1-F2]. It also notes that the meta-analysis included interventions such as NIDCAP, kangaroo care, and developmental care, with NIDCAP described as an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities [N1-F1]. This suggests that caregiver training and fidelity may be built into some interventions through observational guidance and structured caregiving approaches [N1-F1]. The broader evidence base also indicates that caregiver involvement is a central feature of many early intervention programs [N1-F2]. However, the provided evidence does not provide a direct quantitative assessment of fidelity or a controlled comparison of high-fidelity versus low-fidelity implementation [N1-F2].

Differences between home-based and center-based delivery

Home-based and center-based delivery differ in practicality and reach, but the evidence here is not fully direct. The review explicitly notes that interventions may be delivered in the NICU, hospital setting, or home [N1-F2]. Another search result refers to a home-based, post-discharge early intervention program and states that home visits are a convenient and effective form of intervention immediately after discharge because parents or caregivers are generally less confident and may need more support [N6-R3]. A separate search result also refers to a clinician-supported, web-based early intervention program for preterm infants [N6-R2], which implies that technology-assisted or hybrid delivery models are being tested. The provided evidence does not provide a direct comparison of home-based versus center-based delivery outcomes, but it does indicate that both settings are used and that home-based models may be attractive because they can reach families after discharge [N1-F2][N6-R3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that timing during NICU stay is important, caregiver training and fidelity may be embedded in some interventions, and home-based delivery is a practical and sometimes effective model after discharge, but direct comparative evidence on dosage, fidelity, and home versus center-based effects is limited in the provided material [N1-F1][N1-F2][N6-R3].

# Integrated synthesis of evidence on early parental stimulation and motor development in premature infants

## 1. What interventions have been tested and what motor outcomes they target

The evidence base indicates that early parental stimulation interventions are not a single uniform program, but a broad family of approaches often involving parents, families, and caregivers. The most commonly named interventions in the search results include NIDCAP, kangaroo care, developmental care, sensory stimulation, music, and physical therapy [N1-F1]. One review explicitly describes early intervention programs as designed to support parents in promoting the development of their preterm infant, with interventions varying in nature, intensity, setting, and parental involvement [N1-F2]. NIDCAP is particularly highlighted as an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities [N1-F1], showing that many interventions are adapted rather than purely standardized.

Motor and neurodevelopmental outcomes are measured using a mix of standardized and infant-specific tools. The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development are repeatedly referenced as central developmental assessment instruments [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5], with the Bayley-4 described as a standardized assessment tool [N2-R4]. The review evidence also notes that neurobehavioral assessments such as general movements and the Test of Infant Motor Performance (TIMP) are among the most significant predictors of long-term neurodevelopment [N1-F1]. This means that motor outcomes are assessed with both broad developmental scales and more specific motor-performance tools, while neurodevelopmental outcomes are measured with standardized scales [N2-R1][N2-R2][N1-F1].

A key distinction is whether interventions are standardized or adapted for preterm infants. NIDCAP is clearly described as an individualized approach tailored to preterm infants through observational caregiving guidance [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that interventions varied in participants, interventions, and outcome measures across trials, suggesting that many programs are adapted to the specific needs of the infant and family rather than being rigidly standardized [N1-F2]. This matters because adaptation is part of the intervention logic, but it also introduces heterogeneity in how interventions are implemented and measured.

## 2. What the evidence base says about intervention effects and consistency across studies

The evidence is generally mixed but suggestive of some benefit. One systematic review and meta-analysis found that NIDCAP was effective in improving preterm infants’ neurobehavioral and neurological development at two weeks corrected age, while parental participation did not significantly improve neurobehavioral development during NICU hospitalization [N1-F1]. For other interventions, the synthesis showed that effectiveness was either controversial or partially effective [N1-F1]. Another meta-analysis of parent-involved interventions found statistically significant differences in favor of the intervention at 12 and 24 months for mental and performance scales, with weaker evidence at 36 months and no difference at five years [N1-F2]. These results indicate a positive direction of effect, but not uniform across all outcomes or all intervention types.

The strongest evidence comes from randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses. The NIDCAP meta-analysis and the broader parent-involved interventions meta-analysis both relied on randomized trials [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence is also stronger for higher-risk infants and for follow-up at 12 and 24 months, where differences were statistically significant [N1-F2]. However, the evidence is weaker at later follow-up, with no statistical difference at five years in the meta-analysis [N1-F2]. This suggests that the most consistent effects are seen in short-term NICU and early postnatal follow-up, whereas longer-term evidence is less robust.

A major limitation is heterogeneity. The review explicitly notes that the included trials varied in participants, interventions, and outcome measures, and that the review pooled trials with variation in design and outcome measures [N1-F2]. It also states that the overall quality of evidence was low to very low [N1-F1]. Sample sizes are uneven across studies: the NIDCAP meta-analysis combined three studies involving 901 preterm infants [N1-F1], whereas the parent-involved intervention meta-analysis included 25 randomized controlled trials with 3,509 children [N1-F2]. Despite this, the review still reports statistically significant effects at some time points, which suggests that the sample size is sufficient for some comparisons, but not necessarily for all subgroups or outcomes [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Follow-up duration is another important limitation. The review emphasizes that many interventions are evaluated at one year of age or older, raising concerns about confounding factors that may have occurred between NICU discharge and the timing of assessments [N1-F1]. The longitudinal follow-up paper likewise stresses that favorable outcomes at an early age do not necessarily reflect later abilities and that individual trajectories can shift over time [N5-F3]. This means that short-term gains may not reliably predict long-term outcomes [N1-F1][N5-F3].

## 3. How intervention design features affect outcomes

### Timing, frequency, and dosage of stimulation

Timing appears to be an important design feature. The evidence focuses largely on interventions initiated during NICU hospitalization, with effectiveness measured during hospitalization and up to two weeks corrected age [N1-F1]. This suggests that early NICU-based intervention is a major focus of the evidence base. The same review also notes that many interventions are assessed only at one year of age or older, raising concerns about confounding factors occurring after discharge [N1-F1]. While the evidence does not directly quantify frequency or dosage, it implies that timing during NICU stay may matter more than later timing, because the intervention is delivered in the context of the NICU environment where preterm infants are most vulnerable [N1-F1].

### Caregiver training and fidelity

Caregiver training and fidelity are important but only indirectly supported in the provided evidence. The review states that interventions varied in intensity, setting, and parental involvement, and that the review pooled trials with variation in participants, interventions, and outcome measures [N1-F2]. It also notes that NIDCAP is an individualized approach based on observing preterm infants’ behaviors to guide caregiving activities [N1-F1]. This suggests that caregiver training and fidelity may be embedded in some interventions through observational guidance and structured caregiving approaches [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not provide a direct quantitative assessment of fidelity or a controlled comparison of high-fidelity versus low-fidelity implementation [N1-F2].

### Home-based versus center-based delivery

Home-based and center-based delivery differ in practicality and reach, but direct comparative evidence is limited in the provided material. The review explicitly notes that interventions may be delivered in the NICU, hospital setting, or home [N1-F2]. Another source describes home visits as a convenient and effective form of intervention immediately after discharge because parents or caregivers are generally less confident and may need more support [N6-R3]. A separate search result also refers to a clinician-supported, web-based early intervention program for preterm infants [N6-R2], indicating that technology-assisted or hybrid models are being tested. The provided evidence does not provide a direct comparison of home-based versus center-based delivery outcomes, but it does indicate that both settings are used and that home-based models may be attractive because they can reach families after discharge [N1-F2][N6-R3].

Overall, the evidence suggests that timing during NICU stay is important, caregiver training and fidelity may be built into some interventions, and home-based delivery is a practical and sometimes effective model after discharge.
